video_metadata.working_title: MICHIGAN 1969 Cold Case Solved After 35 Years — Justice for Jane Mixer
video_metadata.topic_one_sentence: A 23-year-old University of Michigan law student who arranged a ride home through a campus ride board was found dead in a cemetery near Ypsilanti in March 1969; 35 years later DNA named retired nurse Gary Earl Leiterman, convicted in 2005, but the same lab work also produced the DNA of a man who was four years old in 1969.
video_metadata.primary_emotion_to_evoke: grief turning into unease: justice arrived, but with a question attached

protagonist._instructions: Victim-centred story. Protagonist = Jane Louise Mixer.
protagonist.occupation_or_status: First-year law student at the University of Michigan, living in the Law Quadrangle [1][10]
protagonist.location: Ann Arbor, Michigan; family home in Muskegon, Michigan [1]
protagonist.physical_description: Not used; real archival photo only.
protagonist.background_brief: Daughter of Muskegon dentist Dr. Dan C. Mixer [1]. She was heading home to Muskegon for spring break, and according to accounts of the family story she planned to announce her engagement [10]. She found a ride through a notice on a campus ride board [10][5].
protagonist.psychological_profile: Not documented in verified sources; do not invent.
protagonist.mundane_humanizing_detail: She used the ordinary student system of the time, a ride board, to get home to her parents [10][5].

individuals.name: Jane Louise Mixer
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Murdered on the night of March 20-21, 1969; shot twice in the head and strangled, according to later accounts [8][14]; found March 21, 1969 in Denton Cemetery [1]
individuals.humanizing_detail: Going home to Muskegon for spring break; planned to announce an engagement [10]

individuals.name: Dr. Dan C. Mixer
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Waited for Jane that night; around 11 p.m. he set out in his car to look for her and drove around for several hours, per Maggie Nelson's account to CBS [5]
individuals.humanizing_detail: Described in 1969 as a prominent Muskegon dentist [1]

individuals.name: Maggie Nelson
individuals.role_or_profession: Poet and author, Jane's niece (born after the murder)
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Wrote 'Jane: A Murder' and the 2007 memoir 'The Red Parts' about the reopened case and the 2005 trial; she and her mother spent the summer of 2005 in Ann Arbor for the trial [10][11]
individuals.humanizing_detail: Interviewed the man Jane had been dating when she was killed, per reviews of The Red Parts [19]

individuals.name: John Ruelas
individuals.role_or_profession: Man convicted of killing his mother in 2002
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: His DNA matched a blood spot on Jane's hand, although he was 4 years old in 1969 [7][8]
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Ruled out because of his age; his match is the centre of the contamination debate [7]

collective_victims_if_applicable.group_description: Young women killed in Washtenaw County area 1967-1969 ('Michigan Murders')
collective_victims_if_applicable.total_number_affected: Seven young women found dead within about two years; Jane was the third [1][13]
collective_victims_if_applicable.range_of_impacts: Fear across Ann Arbor and Ypsilanti campuses; ages roughly 13 to 23 [13]

characters.name: Gary Earl Leiterman
characters.role_in_story: Convicted killer; retired nurse, 62 at his 2004 arrest; lived in Ann Arbor at the time of the murder [3][4]
characters.key_actions_they_took: DNA entered into the database after a 2001 arrest for forging prescriptions [9]; arrested November 2004 [3]; convicted of first-degree murder in 2005 after less than three hours of jury deliberation [8]; sentenced to life without parole [6]; maintains innocence [6]

characters.name: John Norman Collins
characters.role_in_story: Eastern Michigan University student convicted in 1970 of the murder of Karen Sue Beineman, 18; long assumed to be Jane's killer but never charged in her death [10][13]
characters.key_actions_they_took: Serving life without parole; held at Marquette Branch Prison per reports; now known as John Norman Chapman; maintains innocence [13]

characters.name: Michigan State Police cold case detective (Det. Sgt. Eric Schroeder / Schroder; spelling varies)
characters.role_in_story: Re-examined old evidence and had the stockings tested for DNA [9]

characters.name: Gary Gabry
characters.key_actions_they_took: Argued lab contamination; sought testimony of DNA expert Dan Krane, which was limited by the court [8]

characters.name: Dan Krane
characters.role_in_story: Wright State University biology professor, defense DNA expert [8]

characters.name: John Wixted
characters.key_actions_they_took: In 2016, after consulting six DNA experts, argued contaminated DNA evidence may have convicted the wrong man [7][16]

events.what_happened: Start of the series of killings of young women later called the Michigan Murders
events.significance: Context of fear in which Jane's case was filed

events.location: University of Michigan campus, Ann Arbor
events.what_happened: Jane Mixer left campus to go home to Muskegon with a ride arranged through a campus ride board
Jane's father, worried she had not arrived, set out in his car to look for her and drove for several hours

events.location: Denton Cemetery, Cross St., about two miles east of Ypsilanti, Wayne County
events.what_happened: Jane's body found just inside a wire fence at an east entrance; first reports said beaten and strangled, a stocking around her neck
events.significance: Discovery; the stockings later yield the DNA

events.what_happened: Police searched for the person Jane had arranged a ride with; it had not been determined whether that man ever picked her up
Karen Sue Beineman, 18, last seen July 23, 1969; John Norman Collins arrested and later convicted (1970) of her murder only
events.significance: Jane's case folded into the 'Michigan Murders'; Collins never charged in her death

events.what_happened: Michigan State Police reopen Jane's case for DNA testing of evidence collected more than 30 years earlier; same year Leiterman arrested for forging prescriptions and his DNA entered into the system
events.significance: The two threads that will meet

events.what_happened: Cold-case DNA analysis yields two male profiles matching the national database: Leiterman (pantyhose) and John Ruelas (blood spot on Jane's hand)
John Ruelas killed his mother; his DNA entered the database; he was 4 years old in 1969

events.date: November 2004 (a Wednesday; AP story dated Nov. 26)
events.what_happened: Gary E. Leiterman, 62, retired nurse, arrested and charged with one count of murder; held without bond

Trial; DNA analyst testifies samples tested same day but in separate parts of lab; handwriting witness calls phone-book writing 'highly probable' Leiterman's; jury convicts of first-degree murder after under three hours
Leiterman sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole
CBS 48 Hours airs 'Deadly Ride' on the case
Maggie Nelson publishes The Red Parts about the reopened case and trial
Psychologist John Wixted, after consulting six DNA experts, argues contamination may have convicted the wrong man; Leiterman seeks new trial, maintains innocence

the_moment.exact_location: Denton Cemetery, Cross Street, about two miles east of Ypsilanti, Michigan
the_moment.what_is_happening: The body of a 23-year-old law student is found just inside the cemetery fence, the morning after she set out for home with a ride from a campus ride board
the_moment.what_makes_it_shocking: She had used the most ordinary student system of her day, and she was placed in the cemetery with her belongings
the_moment.ironic_twist: In 2002 the DNA named two men: a retired nurse and a man who had been four years old in 1969

cold_open_material.central_mystery_question: Who was the driver from the ride board, and can DNA be trusted when it names a four-year-old boy?

the_method.technique_name: STR DNA profiling of preserved 1969 evidence searched against CODIS
step_by_step_explanation: Evidence (pantyhose/stockings, blood spot from hand) preserved since 1969 [7][9]
Re-tested by Michigan State Police around 2001-2002 [15][7]
Profiles uploaded to the national DNA database [7]
Hits: Leiterman (entered after 2001 forgery arrest) and Ruelas (entered after 2002 killing) [9][7]
Ruelas excluded because he was 4 in 1969 [7]
the_method.why_it_worked: The evidence was kept for more than 30 years and Leiterman's profile had entered the database for an unrelated non-violent offence [9]

technical_terms_to_explain.simple_explanation: The FBI's national computer index of DNA profiles from crime scenes and from people arrested for or convicted of certain crimes
DNA from one sample accidentally getting onto another, like a fingerprint left on a glass by the person who washed it
DNA from sweat or skin cells rather than blood or semen; the Leiterman DNA was reported as possibly from sweat, saliva or skin cells [8]

the_method.scale_of_operation: Three samples of Leiterman's DNA reported on the pantyhose [8]

systemic_failure.institution_that_failed: 1969 investigation (tunnel vision toward a serial-killer theory) and, per the defense, the 2002 crime lab
systemic_failure.how_they_were_supposed_to_protect: Identify the ride-board driver; keep lab evidence uncontaminated
systemic_failure.why_they_failed: Jane's death was grouped with the Michigan Murders though it differed (she was shot and placed with her belongings) [9][17]; in 2002 a 4-year-old's DNA appeared on her hand and was never explained [8]
specific_incompetence_examples: Case assumed to be Collins's for about three decades though he was never charged [10]
Ruelas and Mixer samples processed in the same lab on the same day [8]
Handwriting witness had examined only photos [14]
systemic_failure.ironic_details_about_the_failure: The DNA that convicted Leiterman came from the same testing that produced a match to a man who was a small child in 1969

the_investigation.investigating_agency: Michigan State Police; Washtenaw County Prosecutor's Office
the_investigation.initial_wrong_assumptions: That Jane was a victim of the Michigan Murders serial killer [10][13]
the_investigation.key_breakthrough: Database hit on DNA from the pantyhose to Gary Leiterman [9][7]
the_investigation.the_fatal_mistake: His DNA was collected after a 2001 arrest for forging prescriptions [9]

the_confrontation.scene_description: Arrested, charged with one count of murder, held without bond [3][4]
the_confrontation.ironic_or_absurd_details: He was 62 and retired; in 1969 he had lived in Ann Arbor [4]

charges_filed: One count of murder (first-degree murder at trial) [3][8]
legal_resolution.notable_court_testimony: DNA analyst: samples tested same day, technicians in separate parts of lab, quality controls made mix-up unlikely [8]; police lieutenant: phone-book writing 'highly probable' Leiterman's, but examined only photos [14]; defense expert Dan Krane allowed only limited testimony [8]

victim_impact_statements.emotional_impact: Family attended; Maggie Nelson and her mother spent the summer in Ann Arbor [10]

legal_resolution.sentence_received: Life in prison without the possibility of parole [6]
legal_resolution.current_status: Last public reports (2016) show Leiterman serving life and maintaining innocence, seeking a new trial [6][7]. No verified report of exoneration, new trial, or death was found. Verify on Michigan DOC OTIS before publishing.

universal_stakes.why_this_matters_to_viewer: DNA is treated as certainty, yet this case shows it can carry an unexplained error alongside a match
universal_stakes.how_this_could_happen_to_them: Anyone who accepted a ride from a stranger in an era of trust
universal_stakes.lesson_or_warning: Evidence must be kept and labs must be transparent; justice needs both the science and the doubt
universal_stakes.current_relevance: Contamination remains a live issue in forensic DNA [7]
